opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the core motivation is that the split between transactional and analytical systems was always more of a technical limitation than something anyone actually wanted. Historically you had your operational database, Postgres or MySQL or whatever, running the application. Then you had a separate warehouse for analytics, and a whole tangle of ETL pipelines copying data between them. Every one of those pipelines is something that can break, something that adds latency, and another copy of the data you have to govern and secure.

What's changed is mostly on the storage side. With cheap, durable object storage and open formats like Delta and Iceberg, you can separate compute from storage much more cleanly. Then the real question becomes whether you can put a low-latency transactional layer on top of that same storage. You'd want fast point reads and writes, and proper transactions, without giving up the ability to run big scans over the same data. If you can do that, a lot of the plumbing just goes away.

There are a few reasons I'm excited about it. One is freshness. Analytics and especially AI applications increasingly want to act on what's happening right now, not on yesterday's batch. Another is governance. If there's one copy of the data with one set of permissions and lineage, it's a lot easier to reason about who can see what. That matters even more when you have agents reading and writing data. And the third is just simplicity for developers. People don't want to be distributed systems engineers to build an app that also needs a dashboard.

To be fair, it's not free. Transactional and analytical workloads have really different access patterns, so you have to be careful about isolation. A huge analytical query shouldn't hurt your p99 latency on the operational side. A lot of the engineering is in caching, in how you lay out the data, and in keeping the compute for each workload separate even though the storage is shared. But I think the trend is clear. Storage is converging, and the different engines become views over the same data, rather than separate silos you have to keep in sync.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the complexity of separate databases and warehouses, but does not identify losing access to established database ecosystems as a drawback.

r002.rationale: It notes different workload access patterns and the need to protect operational p99 latency, but does not say a unified engine struggles to match specialized-engine performance.

r003.rationale: It describes shared storage with a transactional layer and analytical scans, but does not claim storage unification alone captures nearly all the benefits.

r004.rationale: It mentions Postgres and open formats, but does not explain storing Postgres writes in a shared column-oriented format for direct analytical reads.

r005.rationale: It says ETL pipelines add latency and that shared storage lets analytics scan the same data, supporting immediate analytical availability when the intermediate pipeline is removed.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I should say up front that I don't really think of it as a specific product called "L-TAP" so much as a design principle, and it's one I've believed in since we started working on Delta Lake and what we later called the lakehouse architecture.

The core problem is that for twenty years the industry accepted a split: you run your transactions in one system, you copy the data out through some ETL pipeline, and you analyze it in a completely different system with a different storage format, different governance, different security model. Every one of those copies is a liability. It's stale by the time it lands, it's expensive, and when the numbers don't match between the operational system and the dashboard, somebody spends a week figuring out which pipeline broke.

What changed is that cheap object storage plus an open table format with real ACID semantics gives you a foundation where you don't have to make that copy. Delta's transaction log was really the key insight for us. Once you can do atomic commits, snapshot isolation, and time travel on top of files sitting in S3 or a similar store, you can let a streaming ingest job, a batch ML training job, and a BI query all hit the same tables without stepping on each other.

Now, I want to be careful here. I'm not claiming you run your high-frequency OLTP bank ledger on Parquet files. Latency-sensitive point writes still want a purpose-built engine. What I'm arguing is that the storage layer underneath should be shared and open, so that the analytical side sees transactional changes within seconds, not hours, and so that the same governance applies everywhere. The engines on top can specialize. The data shouldn't have to move.

The other reason I favor it is incentives. When storage is open and shared, you can swap engines without a migration, and vendors have to compete on query performance and features instead of on lock-in. That's good for users, and honestly it's forced all of us, Databricks included, to be better.

r001.rationale: The response discusses avoiding migration and vendor lock-in, but does not identify losing access to established database ecosystems as a drawback of a new unified engine.

r002.rationale: It says latency-sensitive point writes still need a purpose-built engine and that engines can specialize, communicating the performance case for specialized engines.

r003.rationale: It argues that shared, open storage with transactional semantics avoids data copies while allowing specialized engines, governance, and analytics over the same tables.

r004.rationale: It refers to Delta tables and files in object storage, but does not explain that Postgres writes in a shared column-oriented format can be read directly by analytical engines.

r005.rationale: It describes removing the ETL copy and says analytics can see transactional changes within seconds rather than hours.

astra-6.text:
The main appeal is that you don’t have to maintain two separate versions of your data—one for transactions and another for analytics—and then build a pipeline to keep them synchronized. That pipeline adds complexity, and it means your analytical queries are often looking at stale data.

With unified storage, you can simplify that architecture and make fresh transactional data available for analysis. But unified storage doesn’t mean every workload should use the same execution strategy. You still want specialized query processing and resource isolation so a large analytical query doesn’t interfere with latency-sensitive transactions. That’s the balance I find compelling: share the data while giving each workload the execution machinery it needs.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention losing access to established database ecosystems.

r002.rationale: It recommends specialized query processing and resource isolation, but does not state that one engine struggles to match specialized engines’ performance.

r003.rationale: It describes benefits of unified storage, but does not say storage alone captures nearly all the benefits of a unified system.

r004.rationale: It does not mention Postgres writes or a shared column-oriented format.

r005.rationale: It says eliminating the synchronization pipeline makes fresh transactional data available for analysis.

sol-6.1.text:
The main appeal is that you don’t have to move data between separate transactional and analytical systems before you can ask questions about it. That movement adds complexity, and it means your analytics are always looking at a somewhat stale copy. With unified storage, updates and analytical queries can operate on the same underlying data.

Of course, sharing storage doesn’t automatically solve performance isolation. You still need to make sure a large analytical query doesn’t slow down transactions. But I like the direction: let the system manage those different access patterns instead of making every application team build and maintain a data pipeline.

r001.rationale: The response discusses data movement and pipeline maintenance, but does not mention losing access to established database ecosystems.

r002.rationale: It raises performance isolation between queries and transactions, but does not say a single engine struggles to match specialized engines’ performance.

r003.rationale: It favors shared underlying data, but does not state that storage unification alone captures nearly all benefits of a unified system.

r004.rationale: It does not mention Postgres writes or a shared column-oriented format that analytical engines can read directly.

r005.rationale: It says analytics need not wait for data to move from a separate transactional system and can query the same underlying data, avoiding a stale intermediate copy.
